Topic: What is more perilous to a man's judgment: the vanity that makes him trust his own eyes too much, or the custom that makes him trust everyone else's?
Nietzsche — Judgement:
I neither trust vanity nor custom—I question the very will that produces the judgment.

Two herd-moralities in disguise, that is what this question offers me: the vanity that flatters the ego into believing its perception is truth, and the custom that flatters the crowd into believing consensus is truth. Both are evasions of the harder task—the self-overcoming that demands one *create* values rather than inherit or admire them. The vain man merely worships a smaller herd of one; the customary man worships a larger herd of many. Neither has yet asked what Zarathustra asks: by what right do you judge at all, and have you paid for that right in suffering, solitude, and error?

Custom is the more perilous, for vanity at least preserves the ember of a self, however inflated, while custom extinguishes it entirely into the anonymous "one thinks."

*Better a proud eye that errs alone than a borrowed eye that sees nothing of its own.*
Camus — Judgement:
The eyes that trust themselves too much and the ear that trusts everyone else's — both are forms of the same disease.

I have spent my life watching two kinds of men fail. One trusts his own eyes so completely he mistakes clarity for certainty — he sees the world and believes he sees its meaning. The other surrenders to custom, to what has always been said, and calls that surrender wisdom. Both are fleeing the same abyss: that the world is silent and offers no verdict of its own. Vanity at least keeps a man in contact with his own experience, however distorted; custom removes him from experience altogether, asking him to see through dead men's eyes. The absurd man is condemned to judge without a guarantee — but he must judge as himself, not as an inherited chorus.

Custom is the more perilous, for it disguises surrender as safety and never announces itself as an error.

*A man deceived by his own eyes has at least been present for the crime; a man ruled by custom was never in the room.*
Bashō — Judgement:
Vanity errs by trusting a single flash of sight and calling it the whole moon; custom errs by trusting every mouth that has ever spoken of the moon and calling that seeing.

I have walked to Matsushima and to the old pond, and I trust neither the eye alone nor the guidebook alone — I trust the eye disciplined by walking the same ground until the self wears thin and only the frog's plop, the moon's shape remains. Vanity's error is the smaller: it can be corrected by one more journey, one more sitting-still. Custom's error compounds — a man who has never once seen for himself cannot even recognize correction when it arrives, for he has no eye left to check the report against.

Vanity is the more perilous, but only because it is curable; custom's peril is that it forgets a cure was ever needed.

*Better to be fooled by your own eye than blind behind another's.*
Wollstonecraft — Judgement:
Neither the arrogant eye nor the borrowed one governs alone — the two conspire, for vanity is what makes a man mistake his inherited prejudice for the plain evidence of his senses.

Custom does not compete with self-trust; it disguises itself as it. A man raised to believe woman's reason inferior does not feel himself obedient to authority — he feels himself observing a fact, confirmed daily by women denied the education that would have proven otherwise. This is the deeper injury: prejudice that has learned to wear the costume of perception escapes the scrutiny either vanity or humility alone might apply. The tyranny of custom is worse precisely because it recruits the vanity of the individual mind to enforce itself, so that the victim of prejudice believes himself its independent judge.

Custom is the graver danger, because it corrupts the very faculty — private judgment — that could otherwise detect it.

*The mind enslaved to custom does not know it is enslaved, for it has been taught to call its chains eyesight.*
Francis Bacon — Judgement:
Idols of the Tribe and Idols of the Cave contend against Idols of the Marketplace — the eye's own distortion against the borrowed error of the crowd — and the question asks which false light misleads a man further.

The vain man errs alone: his understanding, left to itself, discolours nature according to his own predispositions, yet the error stays bounded by one intellect and may in principle be corrected by comparison with another. The credulous man errs in company: words received from others enter the understanding, settle there, and breed disputes and follies without number, and because the error is shared it wears the appearance of confirmation, growing harder to detect the more universally it is held. Custom does not merely mislead a man — it conscripts him into misleading others, and multiplies a single error into a received opinion mistaken for knowledge itself.

Custom is the more perilous corrupter, for it disguises itself as consensus and forecloses the very doubt that might expose it.

*A man who trusts his own eyes may yet be corrected; a man who trusts the crowd's eyes has surrendered the very faculty by which correction is possible.*
Hume — Judgement:
Vanity precedes custom—self-love is prior and universal; custom is only vanity's habit, formed once repetition has dulled the memory of choosing.

Consider what each corruption actually does. The man ruled by vanity mistakes the vividness of his own impression for its truth—he cannot distinguish a passion felt strongly from a fact established soundly. But the man ruled by custom has merely outsourced this same error to a crowd: he trusts many vain men instead of one. Custom is not humility; it is vanity diffused and thereby hidden from itself, which makes it the more dangerous, since a private conceit can be caught in the mirror of another's disagreement, while a whole society's conceit has no mirror at all.

Custom is the graver peril, precisely because it counterfeits modesty.

*The proud man is wrong alone; the credulous man is wrong in company, and mistakes the company for proof.*
Adam Smith — Judgement:
Both vanity and custom lead a man into error, though the vice is the same disguised in two dresses: partiality to one's own judgment over the judgments of others, whether that self stands alone or hides inside a crowd.

The self-command I prize is not solitary genius but the check of the impartial spectator — the imagined fair witness who corrects both the vain man's self-flattery and the timid man's servility to fashion. The vain man mistakes applause for merit; the man of custom mistakes conformity for merit. Neither has done the harder work: submitting his conduct to that disinterested judge within, who cares for neither his pride nor his popularity, only for what is actually estimable.

Custom is the more perilous fault, for vanity at least announces itself and invites correction, while custom disguises surrender as prudence and is scarcely felt as an error at all.

*The man who bows only to fashion has not escaped vanity — he has merely borrowed it from his neighbours.*
